title: A participant that votes no when it gives up, its recorded runs all steps of the model
summary: A participant that gives up before voting aborts in silence, and the coordinator finds out when its timer fires. A developer has the participant's rule vote no as it gives up, so that the coordinator can abort on the vote, and reworks the scenario that covers it: the coordinator now receives the no and aborts once every vote is in, with no timer. The contract's row gains the effect, the model's `ParticipantTimeout` carries it out, and TLC checks the rule under all seven configurations: the invariants, the liveness property and the refinement hold with and without crashes, the inductive step holds, and the recorded runs are all steps of the model. The state counts of the explored configurations drop, since giving up now leaves the states a no vote does.

change.description: In `Participant.decide`, the `GiveUp` row for `WORKING` changes from `transition(ABORTED)` to `transition(ABORTED, VOTE_NO)`, with the comment that the coordinator can then abort on the vote rather than on its timer. The kernel test and the node test for a participant that gives up expect the no vote, and the scripted scenario in `Traces` in which a participant gives up is reworked: the coordinator receives the no, the third participant votes, and the coordinator aborts once every vote is in, without a timeout. `Coordinator.decide` and `Recovery.decide` are untouched.

risk: Low, and the question a reviewer asks is whether the model's results still apply: the model has a participant that gives up take a step of its own, `ParticipantTimeout`, and a no vote from a participant that was never asked to vote no looks like a case the model may not have. The model carries out whatever the rule's row says, so the question is answered by running it.
explanation: The participant's rule in the model is generated from the regenerated contract, so `ParticipantTimeout` sends what the new row says: `Sends` turns `VOTE_NO` into a no vote in the inbox, exactly what `Vote` sends for a participant that cannot do its part. TLC explores 637 states in the first configuration, 3,084 with the coordinator crashing and 11,641 with the participants crashing too, fewer than the 728, 3,448 and 12,754 of the committed rule, since a participant that gives up now reaches the states a no voter reaches and no others, and the invariants, the liveness property and the refinement of transaction commit hold in all of them. The two inductive configurations admit the same 736 and 18,636 states as before, since the invariant does not mention how a participant came to abort, and the step on the new row lands in an admitted state every time. The recorded runs are regenerated from the patched nodes and the patched scenario, and TLC finds every run to start in the model's initial state and every step to satisfy `EveryStepIsOneOfTheModel`: the step that changed, a participant giving up with a no vote, is the model's `ParticipantTimeout` with the patched rule. The model has the new behaviour as a behaviour it always allowed of a no voter, so everything it proves of the protocol covers it, and the coverage of the first configuration shows the changed row taken.
resolution: Merge. The change narrows the protocol's behaviours to ones the model already had of a no voter, and all seven configurations say so. The scenario that was reworked is the one a reviewer should read: the coordinator aborting on the vote is the point of the change, and it is now a recorded run held to the model on every build.
notes: The two-phase-commit model (`apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla`) is built like Box Office's: the coordinator's state machine is generated from its B8 contract. An example of this model is checked under every configuration the model lists, and its verdict is the first that fails.

Trace validation (`TwoPhaseCommitTrace.cfg`): the Java nodes run through scripted scenarios with crashes injected, the state after each step recorded in the model's variables, and TLC checks every recorded step against the model's next-state relation as an action property. It sees changes to the glue around the kernels that no contract and no other configuration sees.
A participant that votes no when it gives up takes only steps the model has.
provenance: Constructed as the third example of trace validation on the two-phase-commit nodes, to pair with 090 and 091, and regenerated when the participant's rule became the model's third generated operator: a change to the rule that alters what the nodes record, with every recorded step still a step of the model, accepted on the strength of all seven configurations.

references.title: Cirstea, Kuppe, Loillier and Merz, Validating Traces of Distributed Programs Against TLA+ Specifications (2024): the technique, and what it finds that model checking the specification alone does not
Bernstein, Hadzilacos and Goodman, Concurrency Control and Recovery in Database Systems (1987), chapter 7: the participant's recovery procedure in two-phase commit, and the blocking property
Lamport and Gray, Consensus on Transaction Commit: the TCommit and TwoPhase specifications, and Paxos commit, the non-blocking alternative
TLC's action properties ([][A]_v in PROPERTIES): a property of every step, reported with the run up to the offending step
